## Simple explanation

AI evaluation is the process of checking whether an AI model or application
does what it is supposed to do, how well it does it, and where it fails.

## Technical explanation

Evaluation uses defined tasks, datasets or scenarios, metrics, and
interpretation criteria to assess a model or end-to-end system. It can
include automated measurements, human judgments, adversarial tests, and
production monitoring. Evaluations should account for the intended use and
the limitations of each metric.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Models can change behaviour across versions, prompts, data, and deployment
conditions. Repeatable evaluations help compare changes, detect regressions,
and provide evidence about whether a system is appropriate for its intended
use.

## How it works

1. Define intended capabilities, constraints, and failure costs.
2. Build representative test cases and select suitable metrics or rubrics.
3. Run the model or application under controlled conditions.
4. Inspect both aggregate results and individual failures.
5. Repeat after relevant changes and monitor real-world behaviour.

## Practical example

A retrieval-augmented question-answering system can be evaluated separately
for retrieval relevance, answer correctness, citation support, and
latency. A single overall score would hide which component needs improvement.

## Common misconceptions

- A benchmark score is not a complete measure of real-world quality.
- An LLM judge can be useful but may have its own biases and errors.
- Testing only successful examples says little about failure behaviour.
